answers.answer:
In SCOPe 2.08, ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins and manganese catalases are three separate families in ONE superfamily, Ferritin-like (a.25.1, sunid 47240). That superfamily sits in the Ferritin-like fold (a.25, sunid 47239), in class a (all alpha). The families are a.25.1.1 Ferritin (sunid 47241), a.25.1.2 Ribonucleotide reductase-like (sunid 47253) and a.25.1.3 Manganese catalase (T-catalase) (sunid 100951). The same superfamily also holds YciF-like (a.25.1.4), half-ferritin (a.25.1.5), PMT1231-like, MiaE-like, AMB4284-like and Rv2844-like families, plus 'automated matches' (a.25.1.0).

How to read this. Sharing a superfamily is SCOPe's claim of probable common evolutionary origin. The evidence is structural, and often functional too: a conserved four-helix-bundle core, typically carrying a dinuclear metal site with carboxylate and His ligands. The sequences are only remotely similar. The three families are distinct families, not close homologs, because their sequence similarity is low and their functions differ. At family level SCOPe expects clearer sequence or functional relatedness.

The chemistries do differ. Ferritin is a ferroxidase and iron-storage protein: Fe(II) is oxidized by O2 or H2O2 at the diiron site and the iron is mineralized in a 24-mer shell. RNR class Ib/R2 (and related diiron proteins such as PaaC in a.25.1.2) uses a diiron or dimanganese site to make a tyrosyl radical or a high-valent oxidant, which starts radical chemistry in the large catalytic subunit. Mn catalase has a dimanganese site that cycles through Mn(II)/Mn(II) and Mn(III)/Mn(III) states to disproportionate H2O2 into water and O2. So the scaffold is shared but the reaction, metal and biological role are not.

The lesson is that the dinuclear-metal four-helix-bundle scaffold was diversified by divergent evolution into different chemistries. A superfamily assignment does not mean the proteins share function. It supports a shared fold and a plausible metal-binding architecture, nothing more.

Limits. (1) Do not transfer function, substrate, metal preference (Fe vs Mn), redox behavior or oligomeric state between families on superfamily membership alone. Ferritin-like proteins have been reported to differ in metal specificity and reaction, and individual members need their own evidence. (2) Do not use a superfamily or family member as a homology-modelling template for catalytic residues or the active-site geometry of another family without checking ligand conservation. Backbone modelling of the helical core is more defensible than modelling the active site. (3) Family membership is not proof of the same activity even within a family. a.25.1.2 is a heterogeneous family that includes PaaC (a phenylacetic acid degradation protein) alongside RNR R2, and MiaE-like and other families are separate. (4) Choose representatives per family and per protein node (for example a.25.1.1 ferritin vs a.25.1.3 Mn catalase), not one for the whole superfamily. (5) Functional claims need external evidence that I did not retrieve from SCOPe: metal content, activity assays, mutagenesis of ligand residues, and sequence or HMM alignments, for example from PDB, UniProt/literature or Pfam/InterPro. SCOPe supplies the structural classification, not the catalytic mechanism.

The families are a.25.1.1 Ferritin (sunid 47241), a.25.1.2 Ribonucleotide reductase-like (sunid 47253) and a.25.1.3 Manganese catalase (T-catalase) (sunid 100951). The same superfamily also holds YciF-like (a.25.1.4), half-ferritin (a.25.1.5), PMT1231-like, MiaE-like, AMB4284-like and Rv2844-like families, plus 'automated matches' (a.25.1.0).

How to read this. Sharing a superfamily is SCOPe's claim of probable common evolutionary origin. The evidence is structural, and often functional too: a conserved four-helix-bundle core, typically carrying a dinuclear metal site with carboxylate and His ligands. The sequences are only remotely similar. The three families are distinct families, not close homologs, because their sequence similarity is low and their functions differ. At family level SCOPe expects clearer sequence or functional relatedness.

The chemistries do differ. Ferritin is a ferroxidase and iron-storage protein: Fe(II) is oxidized by O2 or H2O2 at the diiron site and the iron is mineralized in a 24-mer shell. RNR class Ib/R2 (and related diiron proteins such as PaaC in a.25.1.2) uses a diiron or dimanganese site to make a tyrosyl radical or a high-valent oxidant, which starts radical chemistry in the large catalytic subunit. Mn catalase has a dimanganese site that cycles through Mn(II)/Mn(II) and Mn(III)/Mn(III) states to disproportionate H2O2 into water and O2. So the scaffold is shared but the reaction, metal and biological role are not.

The lesson is that the dinuclear-metal four-helix-bundle scaffold was diversified by divergent evolution into different chemistries. A superfamily assignment does not mean the proteins share function. It supports a shared fold and a plausible metal-binding architecture, nothing more.

Limits. (1) Do not transfer function, substrate, metal preference (Fe vs Mn), redox behavior or oligomeric state between families on superfamily membership alone. Ferritin-like proteins have been reported to differ in metal specificity and reaction, and individual members need their own evidence. (2) Do not use a superfamily or family member as a homology-modelling template for catalytic residues or the active-site geometry of another family without checking ligand conservation. Backbone modelling of the helical core is more defensible than modelling the active site. (3) Family membership is not proof of the same activity even within a family. a.25.1.2 is a heterogeneous family that includes PaaC (a phenylacetic acid degradation protein) alongside RNR R2, and MiaE-like and other families are separate. (4) Choose representatives per family and per protein node (for example a.25.1.1 ferritin vs a.25.1.3 Mn catalase), not one for the whole superfamily. (5) Functional claims need external evidence that I did not retrieve from SCOPe: metal content, activity assays, mutagenesis of ligand residues, and sequence or HMM alignments, for example from PDB, UniProt/literature or Pfam/InterPro. SCOPe supplies the structural classification, not the catalytic mechanism.
evidence_used: pretrained knowledge of ferritin, RNR R2 and Mn catalase chemistry
